text: Perform server-side authorization for each requested resource and operation using trusted identity and policy data. A hard-to-guess object identifier is not a substitute for an access decision.
Path traversal can make a pathname built from external input resolve outside an intended parent directory. Neutralize special path elements so the operation stays within that directory.

source: OWASP Transaction Authorization Cheat Sheet https://cheatsheetseries.owasp.org/cheatsheets/Transaction_Authorization_Cheat_Sheet.html; Stripe Idempotent requests https://docs.stripe.com/api/idempotent_requests
text: Transaction authorization is enforced on the server. A request idempotency key can relate a retry to an earlier result; it serves a different purpose from an authorization credential, and neither source defines every application's transaction approval policy.
Concurrent read, update, and write operations on shared state can interfere and leave an unexpected result when execution is not synchronized.

Rate limits can apply to a user or tenant across distributed service instances. Fixed-window and sliding-window algorithms and shared state are implementation choices that must match the service's stated quota policy.

Duplicate HTTP parameter names may be interpreted differently by components. This creates a risk when validation and later use select different values; whether it is exploitable depends on the application's parsing and validation behavior.
Integer wraparound can turn a security-critical quota calculation into an incorrect decision when the mathematical result exceeds the stored representation.
Keep access tokens, encryption keys, passwords, and other primary secrets out of application logs and diagnostics. Review both normal and error paths for unintended disclosure.
A webhook signature authenticates a delivery payload; transformations before verification can change the data whose integrity is being checked.
An uploaded filename or Content-Type header can be deceptive. A file may contain active content even when its metadata looks like an approved type.

source: Unicode UAX #15, version 18.0.0 https://www.unicode.org/reports/tr15/tr15-58.html; Unicode UTS #39, version 18.0.0 https://www.unicode.org/reports/tr39/tr39-34.html
text: Unicode NFKC can merge compatibility-equivalent strings. A confusable skeleton tests visual similarity instead; it is not identifier normalization or an application identity-equality rule.

source: OWASP Server Side Request Forgery Prevention Cheat Sheet https://cheatsheetseries.owasp.org/cheatsheets/Server_Side_Request_Forgery_Prevention_Cheat_Sheet.html
text: Constrain server-side requests to approved destinations and schemes. Validate domain and resolved address behavior, including redirects, while retaining legitimate allowed requests.

source: OWASP Cross-Site Request Forgery Prevention Cheat Sheet https://cheatsheetseries.owasp.org/cheatsheets/Cross-Site_Request_Forgery_Prevention_Cheat_Sheet.html
text: Validated anti-CSRF tokens and request-origin checks are established defenses with different deployment assumptions. An application may layer these checks according to its own policy.
For GCM, IV generation must satisfy the uniqueness requirement for each key across messages and execution contexts. A local two-call difference alone does not establish a sound nonce lifecycle.
A signed token's algorithm declaration is untrusted input. Verification must account for which algorithms are supported and which algorithm belongs with a key.
Untrusted serialized data may name object types that an application did not intend to construct. Type handling is part of the deserialization trust boundary.
Parsing a certificate is not enough to trust it. Validate the certificate chain, trust anchor, time and intended identity under the application policy before accepting the peer.

Key rotation needs a policy for issuing, retiring, and retaining keys. An old public verification key may remain useful for archived signatures, so old-key acceptance depends on the artifact and application policy.
Password-based key derivation for storage depends on a specified derivation function, salt, and iteration count. Treat salt and work-factor validation as part of the security contract.

An untrusted search-path setting, including PATH, can redirect the lookup of a critical program or library. The risk depends on whether an outside party can influence the search path used for that lookup.
